Known as the McCain Amendment, it prohibits cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment of anyone in U.S. custody, wherever held, and ties Defense Department interrogations to the Army Field Manual. It was enacted as Title X of the FY2006 defense appropriations act and again in that year's defense authorization.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 109-148](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/109/public/148){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 42 U.S.C. 2000dd](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/42/2000dd?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sec. 1002: Defense Department interrogations limited to techniques listed in the Army Field Manual.
- Sec. 1003: ban on cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment regardless of nationality or location.
- Sec. 1004: legal defense for personnel who relied in good faith on legal advice.
- Sec. 1005: limited federal court review of Guantanamo detention and military commission decisions.

## Why it matters

It was the first statutory limit on post-2001 interrogation practice. Its jurisdiction-stripping language set up the litigation that led to the [Military Commissions Act](mil-commissions-2006.qmd). The Field Manual rule was extended to all agencies in the FY2016 defense authorization.

## Current status

In force as amended. Its limits on habeas review were narrowed by the Supreme Court in Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006) and Boumediene v. Bush (2008).

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}

## In the courts

- [Hamdan](../cases/hamdan-2006.qmd) (2006). Held its bar on habeas jurisdiction did not reach cases already pending.
- [Boumediene](../cases/boumediene-2008.qmd) (2008). Held its review procedures were not an adequate substitute for habeas corpus.
